opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things I think about most right now.

When you're evolving a single file, say a training loop or a small algorithm, the whole program fits comfortably in the context window. The LLM can see everything at once, and you have a fairly tight feedback loop: propose a diff, run the evaluator, get a fitness score, keep or discard. The search space is large but still manageable.

Once you move to an entire codebase, a few things break at the same time. The first is context. You can't just dump a hundred thousand lines into the prompt and expect sensible mutations. So you need some notion of which parts of the code are worth mutating, and that's essentially a credit assignment problem. Where in the system did the improvement or regression actually come from?

The second is coupling. In a real codebase, changes are interdependent. If you change an interface in one module, you might have to change five call sites elsewhere. A single local mutation that looks reasonable might simply not compile, or it might silently break something far away. So the mutation operator has to become much more agentic. It needs to navigate, read, plan multi-file edits, and check consistency, rather than just rewrite one block.

The third is evaluation cost. For a single file you can often run the evaluation in seconds or minutes. For a full system, maybe a whole training pipeline, each fitness evaluation can be very expensive, which means you get far fewer generations. That pushes you toward cheaper proxies, surrogate models, or staged evaluation, where you filter candidates with fast checks before running the expensive stuff. And of course proxies open the door to reward hacking, which gets much harder to spot when the code is large and the model has many more places to hide a shortcut.

Finally there's diversity and archive management. In evolutionary approaches you want to keep a population of interesting variants. With whole codebases, how do you even measure novelty or represent the archive? Storing diffs against a base is one option, but the lineages get messy fast.

So I think the path forward combines coding agents as the mutation operators with a smarter outer loop that decides where to focus, how to evaluate cheaply, and how to keep the search open-ended without it collapsing or gaming the metric. We're seeing early signs that this works, but I'd say it's still very much an open research problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses navigating a codebase and coordinating multi-file edits, but does not suggest preserving its hierarchical structure.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an Aider-style repository map or identify a comparable repository-map abstraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the single-file setting is almost a bit of a toy problem in a sense, right? Something like what we did with the Darwin Gödel Machine or with AlphaEvolve-style setups — you have one file, a few hundred lines, you mark the blocks you want to evolve, and the model gets the whole thing in context. It can read it, it can reason about it, it mutates it, you evaluate, done. The context window basically absorbs the entire problem.

The moment you go to a real codebase, that assumption just breaks. You have tens of thousands of files, you have dependencies that span modules, you have build systems, tests that take an hour to run. And so the first challenge is really a retrieval and localization problem: where should the mutation even happen? The model can't see everything, so you need some mechanism — whether that's embeddings, call graphs, static analysis, or just letting the agent explore — to figure out which parts of the codebase are actually relevant to the thing you're trying to improve.

The second thing, and I think this is underappreciated, is credit assignment. In the single-file case, if you change the function and the score goes up, you know what caused it. In a big codebase, a change in one module can have effects three layers down, or it can break something you didn't even know depended on it. So your fitness signal gets much noisier and much more expensive. Evaluating a mutation might mean running an entire CI pipeline. That means you can afford far fewer samples, and the whole evolutionary loop — which really lives off of cheap, parallel evaluation — gets a lot slower.

And then there's the question of what the mutation operator even looks like. Rewriting a file wholesale is fine when it's three hundred lines. At scale, you need diff-based edits, you need the model to produce patches that are coherent across files, and you need some guarantee the thing still compiles. So you end up moving from "LLM as mutation operator" to something much more like an agent with tools — it reads, it searches, it runs tests, it edits incrementally. The evolutionary framing is still there — you keep a population, you archive diverse solutions, you select — but each individual step is now a long-horizon agentic trajectory rather than a single forward pass.

What I find exciting about this is that it also forces you to think about the codebase as something with structure you can exploit. You can evolve at different granularities — functions, modules, architectural decisions — and you can maintain an archive not just of code but of insights about the code: "this subsystem is brittle," "this test is flaky." That meta-knowledge becomes part of what gets inherited across generations. I think that's where the open-ended version of this really starts to look different from what we've done so far.

r001.rationale: The response says codebase structure can be exploited and proposes evolving at function, module, and architectural granularities, conveying that its hierarchy is useful.

r002.rationale: It mentions retrieval, call graphs, static analysis, and agent exploration, but does not identify an Aider-style repository map.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is that a useful mutation stops being a local operation. In a single file, you can give the model the code, ask it to change something, and evaluate the result. Across a codebase, a change in one place might require coordinated changes elsewhere—an interface changes, its callers need updating, and the tests might need to reflect that.

So you need some mechanism for deciding what context the model sees and where it should intervene. Giving it the entire repository doesn’t automatically solve that problem. It has to identify which pieces matter for the proposed change.

And then there’s the evaluation side. Can you cheaply tell whether a mutation is valid, and whether it actually improves the thing you care about? If every candidate requires an expensive end-to-end run, your search becomes very slow. So I’d see context selection, coordinated edits, and efficient feedback as tightly connected parts of the challenge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coordinated changes across files and selecting relevant context, but does not suggest preserving the codebase’s hierarchical structure.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify an Aider-style repository map or an equivalent repository-map abstraction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is maintaining coherence across all the changes. With a single file, you have a fairly compact object that you can mutate and evaluate. With an entire codebase, a change in one place might require changes to interfaces, callers, or tests somewhere else. So the mutation becomes a coordinated set of edits rather than a local rewrite.

Then there’s the feedback problem. Can you cheaply determine whether a candidate still works, and whether it actually improves the objective you care about? If every mutation requires running a large test suite or an expensive experiment, your search becomes very slow.

So I’d frame it as two coupled problems: giving the model enough context to propose coherent changes, and building an evaluation loop that makes searching over those changes practical.
